list.listitem: Physical examination typically reveals salivary gland pain and swelling, most often in the parotid gland, that may be unilateral or bilateral. Malaise, fever, and orchitis in males are common. C
Mumps is best prevented by vaccination; two-dose vaccination is 88% (range 31% to 95%) effective at preventing the disease. (CDC) A
No antiviral treatment for mumps is available. C
No reliable data are published on absolute infertility rates in men with unilateral or bilateral orchitis, but complete sterility is considered rare. C

background.definition: Mumps is a viral infection that often presents with painful enlargement of the salivary glands accompanied by fever, muscle pain, headache, and malaise.

list.listitem: Prior to vaccine, 185,691 cases were reported in 1967. In 1995, only 906 cases were reported.

From January 2016 to June 2017, US health departments reported 150 outbreaks with 9,200 cases to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), including households, schools/universities, athletics teams/facilities, and workplaces.

Outbreaks have occurred among immunized populations. In one study of serologic evidence of mumps virus infection in vaccinated children, investigators found an attack rate of 7% to 10% compared to 2.7% based on clinical symptoms.

Recent incidence rates vary from year to year from several hundred to several thousand; in 2012, there were 229 cases; in 2014, there were 1,151 cases, and in 2019 (Jan to Oct) 2,618 cases were reported to the CDC.

In a study of 101 sporadic cases of parotitis occurring in 8 jurisdictions throughout the United States, 17% tested positive for mumps IgM. Of 38 specimens positive for a single virus, most were positive for Epstein-Barr virus (23) followed by human herpesvirus (HHV)-6B (10); none were positive for Mumps virus.
In a recent review of hospital admissions for meningitis in England, meningitis attributed to mumps was virtually eliminated following the institution of vaccines containing mumps.

In 2005, one report noted that for a cohort of children born in 2001, receipt of the usual childhood vaccines resulted in a cost savings of $9.9 billion in direct costs and $43.3 billion in societal costs. Cost savings for individual vaccines were not determined.
Prior to immunization, mumps infection numbered among the most common causes of sensorineural deafness in children.
Sequelae of mumps-related meningoencephalitis include seizures, aqueductal stenosis, hydrocephalus, cranial nerve palsies, paralysis, and deafness.
A rare sequela of orchitis is infertility.

Mumps is caused by a single-stranded RNA virus in the Paramyxoviridae family; only one serotype is known. This family includes measles/rubella, parainfluenza, metapneumovirus, respiratory syncytial viruses, and Nipah and Hendra viruses.
Mumps is spread via the respiratory tract by fomites and respiratory secretions.
The incubation period is between 14 and 24 days.

The virus has been isolated from saliva from 7 days prior to and up to 9 days after parotitis onset, although the infectious period is considered to occur from 2 days prior to 5 days after parotitis onset. (CDC)

The recommended schedule for MMR or measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella (MMRV) vaccination is two doses, one administered at 12 to 15 months of age and the other at 4 to 6 years of age.
B The two doses are 88% (range 31% to 95%) effective at preventing the disease. (CDC)
Infection may occur in previously vaccinated individuals. B
The main source of prevention is vaccination with MMR or the MMRV vaccine.

At least one dose of MMR is between 69% and 81% effective in preventing clinical mumps for the vaccine prepared with Jeryl Lynn mumps strain and between 70% and 75% effective for the vaccine containing the Urabe strain.

The recommended schedule is two doses, one administered at 12 to 15 months of age and the other at 4 to 6 years of age. The two doses are 88% (range 31% to 95%) effective at preventing the disease. (CDC)

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 3615 RCTs, cohort studies, or longitudinal studies reporting the immunogenicity and persistence of MMR vaccines found an overall seroconversion rate of 93.3% (95% CI 91.1-95.2; I2=94·9%) for mumps when excluding the Rubini strain and 91.1% (95% CI 87.4-94.1; I2=96·6%) for mumps when including the Rubini strain. The overall annual waning rate for mumps was 0.024 (95% CI 0.016-0.039).

A third dose of MMR, offered to 6th- to 12th-grade students in a northeastern US religious community (accepted by 80.6%) that had experienced a large mumps outbreak despite high 2-dose MMR vaccine coverage, resulted in a significant reduction in mumps attack rate for students from 4.9% in the prevaccination period to 0.1% after vaccination.

In another study, a third dose of the mumps vaccine, given during an outbreak on a college campus, was associated with a reduced risk of subsequent infection.The attack rate for those given a third dose of vaccine was 6.7 vs. 14.5 cases/1000 persons for those who'd received only 2 doses (hazard ratio 0.22; 95% CI 0.12-0.39).

The recommended catch-up schedule for those who have passed their 4 to 6 years window and have not been immunized is: two doses of MMR or MMRV spaced 1 month apart. For those who have not reached the 4 to 6 years window, the MMR may be co-administered with all other childhood vaccinations.
In children who have not reached their 13th birthday, the second varicella component must be spaced at least 3 months from the first varicella dose, so the MMRV may not be convenient for catch up.
Because mumps vaccine is cultured in chicken embryo cell culture, individuals with true anaphylaxis to chicken egg should not receive the vaccine.
MMR and MMRV are contraindicated in pregnant women. Women intending to become pregnant should allow 28 days after immunization before attempting pregnancy.

Individuals with specific concerns, such as immunosuppression, cancer treatment, solid organ or bone marrow transplant, warrant adherence to specific immunizations guidelines that are also available from Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. In one study, immunosuppressed patients with inflammatory bowel disease had similar sustained antibody concentrations after vaccination with two-dose MMR vaccine that were comparable to healthy controls.

MMR vaccination is associated with the development of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Risk appears greatest in children who receive the vaccine at 12 to 15 months of age. The risk for developing chronic persistent ITP in children is low (<10% of affected cases). There is a small increased risk of aseptic meningitis and febrile seizure with MMRV vaccine; compared with giving separate MMR + varicella vaccines, there is 1 additional febrile seizure for every 2300 to 2840 doses.
The CDC recommends using separate MMR and varicella vaccines for first vaccinations to decrease the possibility of febrile seizure; MMRV may be administered for the second dose. 33 Overall, serious vaccine-associated side effects are extremely rare.
There is no epidemiologic evidence that links MMR vaccination with allergic diseases such as asthma and atopy, diabetes, autism, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Authors of a National cohort study of 657,461 children in Denmark reported a fully adjusted autism hazard ratio of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.85 to 1.02) for MMR-vaccinated vs. MMR-unvaccinated children; this adds to the evidence of no increased risk for autism following MMR vaccination.

To encourage vaccination, investigators in one RCT with142 subjects found use of a parent meeting in addition to an information pamphlet increased vaccination rates over the pamphlet alone (93% vs. 73%), although both decreased parental decisional conflict. Emphasizing direct benefits to the child may increase vaccine uptake.
Providers should seek opportunities to offer vaccination to appropriate individuals such as during visits for wellness care, chronic care, and pretravel consultation.

Diagnosis is based largely on clinical findings. Physical examination typically reveals salivary gland swelling, most often the parotid gland that may be unilateral or bilateral. Adolescent males often have orchitis. C
Previous immunization does not definitively rule out mumps. C
Laboratory testing using culture, polymerase chain reaction (PCR), acute and convalescent IgG levels, or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) testing is helpful to confirm diagnosis. C

Typical findings on history include malaise, loss of appetite, and recent exposure to mumps. First signs are usually salivary, notably parotid gland swelling and pain, although up to 30% of infections are subclinical.

A history of attendance at camp, college, or other group activity involving close living conditions increases the diagnostic likelihood. Previous childhood immunization does not definitively rule out the possibility of mumps.
Physical examination typically reveals parotid gland swelling and tenderness. Salivary gland swelling may be unilateral or bilateral.

Orchitis occurs in approximately 20% to 30% of unvaccinated postpubertal males and 6–7% of vaccinated postpubertal male mumps patients.(CDC) In 60% to 83% of males with mumps orchitis, only one testis is affected and infertility is rare.

Complications of mumps include meningoencephalomyelitis, orchitis, oophoritis, aseptic meningitis, arthritis, thyroiditis, mastitis, glomerulonephritis, myocarditis, thrombocytopenia, cerebellar ataxia, or transverse myelitis.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or ELISA testing can confirm the diagnosis. Serum IgG present at the initial phase of illness indicates old infection or exposure.

CDC recommends use of real-time reverse-transcription (RT-PCR) testing or mumps culture to confirm mumps in a patient with an acute illness and one of the following features: acute parotitis or other salivary gland swelling, lasting at least 2 days, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, hearing loss, orchitis, oophoritis, mastitis or pancreatitis.

Real-time RT-PCR assay is highly specific and correlates well with results of viral culture. The mumps genome contains 7 genes that are candidates for detection of the mumps virus. A rapid, one-step PCR test against the SH (small hydrophobic protein) gene demonstrated a 100% correlation with positive cultures from buccal swabs as well as 100% correlation with negative cultures.

The optimal specimen for PCR testing is obtained by buccal swab obtained within 3 days of illness onset. Massaging the salivary gland area approximately 30 seconds prior to swabbing the buccal mucosa/parotid duct can assist in obtaining secretions from the infected gland. In patients in patients presenting with orchitis or meningitis, urine or cerebrospinal fluid specimens may be useful for diagnosis in addition to oral specimens.
ELISA tests are also available for rapid diagnosis. Variability in ELISA tests from different manufacturers was reported to range in sensitivity from 24% to 51% and specificity of an average of 82%.
The presence of serum mumps IgM, a significant rise in immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibody titer in acute- and convalescent-phase serum specimens, and IgG seroconversion can aid in diagnosis.

Serum IgM levels indicate acute infection but may not be elevated in early phase of mumps. British investigators report an IgM enzyme immunoassay that uses a recombinant mumps nucleoprotein to detect IgM in serum and oral samples with a 98.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity.
Amylase may be elevated because of salivary gland involvement. Lipase may be elevated in the patient with pancreatic involvement.
Lumbar puncture in patients with signs of meningitis or encephalitis usually shows aseptic meningitis with 0 to 200 mononuclear cells/cubic mm.
Live virus may be cultured from the throat as well as CSF and urine.

Molecular epidemiologic surveillance through virus genotyping is used help track transmission pathways of mumps strains circulating in the United States and can distinguish wild-type mumps virus from vaccine virus. (CDC)
Suspect mumps in a person with parotid gland swelling, malaise, and fever.

The diagnosis is confirmed by RT-PCR testing or mumps culture in combination with clinical data of an acute illness and one of the following: acute parotitis or other salivary gland swelling, lasting at least 2 days, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, hearing loss, orchitis, oophoritis, mastitis or pancreatitis.
Perform lumbar puncture for patients with signs of meningitis or encephalitis.
Treatment is largely supportive. Patients with decreased oral intake may need IV hydration. C
No recommended antiviral treatment for mumps is available.
Case studies using interferon-alpha-2B for the treatment of mumps orchitis to prevent testicular atrophy have been published, but quasiexperimental or randomized trials are lacking.
Treatment for severely painful orchitis includes scrotal elevation, fever reduction, and pain medication.

Hospitalization generally is not required unless a patient presents with possible meningitis or encephalitis, which requires diagnostic evaluation and preliminary treatment before ruling out bacterial meningitis.
Supportive care may be necessary for dehydration secondary to decreased oral intake.
Patients with sequelae from meningoencephalitis need follow-up for potential neurological complications, including hydrocephalus and hearing impairment.

The prognosis in uncomplicated mumps is good, especially in prepubertal children. Complications of meningitis, meningoencephalitis, and neurologic sequelae are rare and no mumps-related deaths have been reported in the U.S. during recent mumps outbreaks. B
No reliable data are published on absolute infertility rates in males with unilateral or bilateral orchitis, but it is considered rare. C
Vaccination in pregnancy is contraindicated.
Maternal mumps in the first trimester may increase the risk of spontaneous pregnancy loss.
No congenital malformations have been linked to maternal mumps infection.

In the general population of mostly vaccinated women, the estimated duration of protection by maternal antibodies among infants is 3.3 months for measles, 2.7 months for mumps, 3.9 months for rubella, and 3.4 months for varicella.
